description: Replay and diff, spec section 9: what a replay compares (9.1), what a difference report contains and in what order (9.2), and how two values at one position are compared (9.3). A case supplies the two sides of a comparison, `recorded` and `replayed`, each a section 8 run record given as its section 7 provenance record plus its rows in the order `rows.jsonl` holds them. A row value is a JSON string, a finite JSON number, or 8.2's wrapper `{"nonfinite": t}`. `expect.matched` is whether the report matched, `expect.record_unfinished` is whether the record it compared holds no summary (8.4) -- false throughout this file, since every case writes two finished records, and an unfinished one is a contract test rather than a vector, since no input/output pair expresses a run that died -- and `expect.differences` is the report's differences, in order: each names a position by `cell` and `key` -- `cell` is null for a member of the determinism contract, and `key` is null for a cell that holds no values and is on one side only -- and carries `recorded` and `replayed`, where a null at a row position means the position is absent and a null at one of the four members is the member's own value (7.1), which equals only another null (9.3). `input.derivation` says which clause of section 9 the expectation comes from; it is prose for the reader, not data an implementation consumes.
source: Hand-derived from spec section 9. Every expectation is read off a clause: 9.1 for what is and is not compared (the four determinism-contract members and the rows; never `environment`, `run_id` or `class`), 9.2 for the shape and order of a report and for its treatment of a position only one side holds, and 9.3 for comparison by kind, exact string equality, the non-finite wrapper compared by the value it names, the null that equals only another null at a determinism-contract member, and the float tolerance. The float cases are evaluated by hand against 9.3's formula |a - b| <= max(1e-9 * max(|a|, |b|), 1e-12), and each one's `derivation` states the difference and the bound so a reader can check the arithmetic without running anything: 5.000000413701855e-10 against a bound of 1.0000000005000001e-9 for the matching pair, about 1e-6 against about 1e-9 for the differing one, and 1e-13 and 1e-11 against the absolute floor of 1e-12 for the two near-zero pairs. Every digest is quoted rather than invented: `sha256:44136fa3...` and `sha256:74234e98...` are conformance/hashing/content.json's `empty-object` and `null`, `sha256:9d7a9f8a...` its `spec-2.2-fingerprint-example`, `sha256:12ae32cb...` its `empty-string` and `sha256:d3626ac3...` its `key-order-does-not-change-hash`, while `sha256:e3b0c442...` is the published SHA-256 of the empty string (FIPS 180-4, RFC 6234). A `code_sha` is a synthetic 40-character lowercase hex value, as in conformance/lab/provenance.json. No expectation in this file was produced by running this kit, and no implementation of section 9 existed when it was written (CLAUDE.md rule 2).

input.derivation: 9.2: a report matched if and only if it carries no difference. Every compared position holds the same value on both sides.

9.2: a position both sides hold whose values differ is one difference carrying both. 9.3: |0.93 - 0.91| = 0.02, and the bound is max(1e-9 * 0.93, 1e-12) = 9.3e-10, so the values differ. `loss` is identical on both sides and so is not a difference.

7.2 and 9.1: `environment` MUST NOT be compared, and two records differing only in `environment` MUST NOT be reported as a divergence. Every member of 7.4's table differs here, platform, runtime version and accelerator included.

9.1: `run_id` is opaque and 7.1 says two records differing only in it describe the same re-execution; `class` classifies how a run was made rather than what it produced. All four determinism-contract members are equal and the rows are equal, so there is nothing to report.

9.3: a `null` is a fourth kind and equals a `null` and nothing else, so two records that both had no lockfile and whose code no git commit names do not differ at `deps_hash` or `code_sha` -- there is no value either side ever had. 7.1 makes those the two null-able members and 7.3 makes these nulls exactly what a `provenance-only` run carries, so this is the ordinary case rather than an exotic one: an implementation reading 9.3's other three kinds as exhaustive would report this replay as diverged at both members.
9.1: `deps_hash` is in the determinism contract of 7.1, so a replay compares it. 9.2: a determinism-contract difference carries `cell` null and the member name as `key`. The rows are equal.

9.2: the determinism-contract members come first, in the order of 7.1's table. The `null` on the replayed side of `deps_hash` and `code_sha` is the member's value, which 7.1 permits, not an absence; 7.3 is why that side is `provenance-only`.
9.2's order: the determinism-contract members first, then the positions of the record's rows.

9.3: a non-finite value is compared by the value its wrapper names, so NaN compares equal to NaN for the purposes of a replay. IEEE 754 equality would report a difference between a run and that same run.
9.3: a non-finite value and a finite number are two kinds, and two values of different kinds differ.
9.3: Infinity equals Infinity, and Infinity and -Infinity differ.

9.2: a cell only one side holds appears as one difference per value it holds, so every unaccounted-for value is named; the `null` says the position is absent, since a row value is never null (8.2). The order is each row's `values` order, and 8.1 makes every document in a record canonical JSON, so 4.1 sorts `grad_norm` before `loss` however the run produced them.

9.2's order: every position of the record's rows first, then the positions only the re-execution holds. The two differences are in different cells, so an implementation that grouped a shared cell's replay-only values beside its recorded ones would emit this pair the other way round. |0.25 - 0.75| = 0.5 against a bound of max(1e-9 * 0.75, 1e-12) = 7.5e-10, so `cell-b`'s `loss` differs.

9.2: positions only the re-execution holds come after the record's, in the order its own rows give them, and such a cell appears as one difference per value it holds -- two here, so the count and the order both bite. 8.1 makes the re-execution's rows canonical JSON too, so 4.1 sorts `grad_norm` before `loss`.

9.2: 8.2 permits an empty `values`, so such a cell has no (cell, key) position and MUST still be reported: one difference naming the cell with `key`, `recorded` and `replayed` all null. A difference with both values null is exactly this case.
9.2: a position only one side holds carries that side's value with null on the other, whether or not the cell itself is shared.

9.3: |1.0 - 1.0000000005| is 5.000000413701855e-10 in binary64, and the bound is max(1e-9 * 1.0000000005, 1e-12) = 1.0000000005000001e-9, so the values are equal. This is the reassociation 7.2 says a second machine may introduce.
9.3: |1.0 - 1.000001| is about 1e-6 and the bound is about 1e-9, so the values differ. A change in the sixth significant figure is a moved value, not noise.

9.3: the relative part gives 1e-9 * 1e-13 = 1e-22, which no non-zero difference could pass, so the absolute part decides: 1e-13 <= 1e-12, and the values are equal. This is why the tolerance has an absolute part at all.
9.3: max(1e-9 * 1e-11, 1e-12) = 1e-12, and 1e-11 > 1e-12, so the values differ. The absolute part is a floor, not an amnesty.
9.3: values are compared by kind first, so the string "0.5" and the number 0.5 are a difference however alike they look.
9.3: two strings are equal only if they are the same sequence of code points; nothing is normalised, trimmed or case-folded. `note` is identical and so is not a difference.
